_comment: Per-name classification of every DRIFTED group reported by
MUST appear here exactly once, classified as either:
`reason` names the language-specific fact that justifies it.
- "tracked": a genuine unreconciled divergence. `task` names the
task filed to fix it (owning package's own current .tasks/phase-NN/).
Zero unclassified entries is the bar -- this file's entry count MUST
equal the live report's drifted_count exactly. Regenerate the name
list from a fresh gate run before editing; never hand-maintain drift.

_api_function_reserved_names.reason: The two bodies are byte-identical code (`to_snake_case(str(fn.name))` keyed against `f"the API helper function '{fn.name}'"`, one dict comprehension over `api.functions.values()`); the only observed difference is documentation: dotnet's docstring names its own downstream renderer `build_api_function_helpers` and documents that the controller re-cases every claimed name with `to_pascal_case` (C# method-naming convention), while java's docstring names `build_api_functions` and documents `to_camel_case` (Java method-naming convention) as the re-casing step applied later.

_apply_param_tag_descriptions.reason: Python mutates `path_params`/`query_params`/`body_param` row dicts IN PLACE (returns `None`), looking each `@param` target up through `_declared_parameter_python_names` (which maps the raw DSL name to `sanitize_python_identifier(p.name.snake)`, since python's rows are keyed by the sanitized, keyword-safe identifier) and raising a SECOND, distinct `GenerationError` when a declared parameter has no matching row because it "may have been absorbed into a multipart plan" -- a case with no typescript equivalent. TypeScript instead builds and RETURNS three fresh values (`api_params`, `api_queries`, `api_body_description_literal`) as a 3-tuple, classifying each tag by raw name membership in `path_names`/`query_names`/`body_param_source_name` sets with a single generic else-raise, and its error text omits python's "Fix: correct the @param name, or remove the tag" remediation sentence entirely.

collapsibility.reason: the two differ in return architecture, not a swappable fact -- python threads mutable row dicts by reference (matching the existing wire_name-is-defined pattern its own docstring cites from `_endpoint_handler_params.py`) and distinguishes 'not declared' from 'declared but multipart-absorbed' as two raise sites, while typescript builds and returns fresh row lists with one collapsed raise site; reconciling mutate-vs-return and a raise-site python has that typescript lacks needs the shared function itself to branch on which data-flow style to produce, which no listed mechanism (casing, type-map, dependency table, signature shape, or raise-site text) addresses.

_build_fields_context.reason: Both are two-line delegates to the already-shared `datrix_codegen_common.algorithms.nosql_fields_context.build_fields_context`, whose own docstring names `resolve_python_type` as the one genuine per-language fact this hoist takes as an explicit parameter. Python passes its bound `self._resolve_nosql_python_type`, which resolves a canonical DSL type to a Pydantic runtime type name + `import_stmt` and raises `GenerationError` on an unmapped canonical type (python's document model embeds a runtime type string in the class body); typescript passes `resolve_python_type=None` because its plain TS interface needs only the canonical DSL type name, resolved later by the template's own type-mapping lookup.

_build_registry.reason: All three bodies are byte-identical single-line delegates -- `return build_seed_registry(seed_documents)` -- to the shared `datrix_codegen_common.algorithms.seed_registry.build_seed_registry`. The only observed difference is Python-source type-hint precision: dotnet's parameter is typed `tuple[SeedDocument, ...]` while java's and python's are typed `tuple[Any, ...]`, plus trivially different docstring wording.

_build_upgrade_op_for_entity_comment_cha.reason: FluentMigrator (dotnet) has no cross-dialect 'set table comment' operation, so dotnet hand-builds raw SQL via `_set_table_comment_sql` (dialect-branching MySQL `ALTER TABLE...COMMENT` vs Postgres `COMMENT ON TABLE`), wraps both the new- and old-value statements as `_csharp_verbatim` strings for `Execute.Sql`/reverse `Execute.Sql`, and needs an `orm_resolver: EfCoreTypeResolver` purely to read `.dialect`. Alembic (python) has a native `create_table_comment`/`drop_table_comment` operation, so python's adapter -- per its own docstring, "never hand-writes DDL for it" -- just returns `comment_literal`/`existing_comment_literal` via Python's `repr()`, needs no dialect parameter at all, and its `UpgradeOp.kind` is the distinctly-named `set_table_comment` versus dotnet's shared generic `set_comment` kind (reused for both table- and column-comment ops).

collapsibility.reason: the divergence is which migration framework owns comment DDL at all -- FluentMigrator has no comment primitive so dotnet must synthesize dialect-specific raw SQL strings, while Alembic's native op needs only a literal value; a shared builder would have to either fabricate raw SQL nobody asked for on the Alembic side or suppress dotnet's dialect branching, neither of which any casing/type-map/dependency/signature/raise-site pattern expresses.

_build_upgrade_op_for_field_comment_chan.reason: Same FluentMigrator-vs-Alembic split as the entity-comment op, but the column case adds MySQL's specific restriction: MySQL has no standalone column-comment statement, so dotnet's `_set_column_comment_sql` must restate the column with its CURRENT type and nullability (`fm_col.efcore_or_sql_type`, `col.nullable`) inside `ALTER TABLE...MODIFY COLUMN`, sourced through `_column_from_snapshot(col, orm_resolver)` -- omitting either would silently rewrite the column, per that function's own docstring. Python's `op.alter_column(..., comment=...)` instead needs only `existing_type` (read from the CURRENT snapshot, exactly as `alter_column_type` reads it, per its docstring) because some backends restate the column to change it, with no dialect-specific branching and no `orm_resolver` parameter at all.

collapsibility.reason: unlike the entity-comment pair, the column case additionally forces dotnet to thread type AND nullability through a MySQL-specific column-restatement workaround that Alembic's native `alter_column(comment=...)` op absorbs internally -- a second, column-specific ORM-capability gap layered on the same table-vs-native-op split, so collapsing it would need the shared function to know MySQL's restate-on-comment quirk, which is a raw-SQL-synthesis fact no listed mechanism owns.

_collect_type_imports.reason: The two functions share a name but perform unrelated operations in unrelated subsystems. Java's version recursively walks a `DatrixType` AST node (entity/struct types) via a `TestValueContext` carrying a `type_resolver`, returns a fresh `set[str]` of Java import statements needed to compile a generated JUnit test-value expression, recurses into nested `StructType` fields with cycle protection via a `seen: frozenset[str]`, and raises `GenerationError` when no `type_resolver` was supplied. Python's version takes an already-rendered SQLAlchemy type-expression STRING (`sa_expr: str`, e.g. `sa.Integer()` or `geoalchemy2.Geography(...)`), string-matches it against `DIALECT_SA_IMPORTS` (or a `geoalchemy2.` prefix check) to find the needed migration-file import, and mutates a caller-supplied `into: set[str]` in place (returns `None`) -- no AST traversal, no recursion, no context object, no resolver, no exceptions.

collapsibility.reason: there is no shared operation to hoist -- java collects compile-time import statements for a generated test-value expression by recursing an AST type, while python extracts a migration-file import from an already-rendered SQLAlchemy type string by pattern-matching; disjoint input types (`DatrixType` vs `str`), disjoint output conventions (return a fresh set vs mutate a passed-in set), and disjoint domains (entity test generation vs DB migration schema). The two are only lexically identical; the fix is renaming one (e.g. java's to `_collect_test_value_type_imports`, or python's to `_collect_sa_type_imports`) so the drift detector stops pairing unrelated functions.

_column_default_sql.reason: dotnet's version (4 params: col, default, sql_type, table_name, dialect) checks default.kind first (server_function/generated -> local _translate_server_function_default) and only then checks col.type.kind == 'enum', because FluentMigrator's caller already resolved a single raw sql_type string per column via EfCoreTypeResolver; it classifies literals by lowercase-prefix-matching that already-resolved sql_type string and raises GenerationError. typescript's version (6 params, with an added snapshot and a second sql_dialect string alongside the SQLDialect object) checks col_def.type.kind == enum FIRST -- before even looking at default.kind -- because MikroORM's CREATE TABLE spans multiple SQL dialects and needs the snapshot to resolve enum members; its literal classification goes through _literal_default_class, which cross-checks SQL_TYPE_MAP consistency across every SUPPORTED_DIALECTS entry (falling back to 'unsupported' if dialects disagree) rather than string-matching one resolved type, and it raises ValueError instead of GenerationError, and routes server-evaluated defaults through the shared datrix_codegen_sql.column_builder.call_source_default_to_sql rather than a local translator.

collapsibility.reason: the two functions differ in dispatch ORDER (kind-then-type vs type-then-kind), in exception type raised (GenerationError vs ValueError), in how a literal's SQL class is decided (single resolved-type string match vs a dialect-consistency check over every supported dialect), and in parameter count/shape (typescript needs snapshot+dual dialect reps dotnet doesn't carry) -- there is no shared classification table or predicate left to hoist once each language's own dialect-resolution architecture is subtracted out.

_connection_surface_declared_types.reason: Both build the identical {ck.key: ck.value_type} mapping over surface.keys with no branching; python writes it as an explicit loop into a pre-declared dict with an inline comment noting the two real values ('String'/'Integer'), typescript writes the same mapping as a one-line dict comprehension -- identical semantics, differing only in loop-vs-comprehension authoring style.

_connection_surface_defaults.reason: The function bodies are byte-identical (build defaults[ck.key] = ck.default for every key with a non-None default); typescript's docstring adds an extra paragraph explaining that a credential/secret key can never appear here (secrets resolve through ConnectionSecret handles instead), a documentation-only addition with no corresponding code difference, and python's surface parameter is typed as a bare DerivedConnectionSurface while typescript's is a quoted forward reference (both resolve to the same shared datrix_common domain type).

_connection_value_type.reason: java and typescript declare byte-identical bodies -- both look up ck.value_type in their own private module-level _VALUE_TYPE_FOR_CONNECTION_KEY dict (String/Integer/Boolean -> ConfigValueType) and raise the same-shaped GenerationError on a miss; the only textual difference is the language name embedded in the error message ('Java ConfigValueType mapping' vs 'TypeScript ConfigValueType mapping') and the ck parameter's type annotation (bare ConnectionKey vs a quoted forward reference). Both docstrings explicitly note this is a deliberate fail-loud mirror of each other and NOT of python's own same-named helper, which silently falls back an unmapped type to STRING instead of raising.

_create_enum_type_sql.reason: python's version accepts an explicit schema: str | None parameter and renders a schema-qualified type name via _qualified_pg_identifier(name, schema) so the CREATE TYPE lands in the DSL block's own declared PostgreSQL schema (matching its tables) rather than wherever the migration connection's search_path happens to point; dotnet's version takes no schema parameter at all and always renders a bare, unqualified sql_quoted_identifier(type_name). This is not a stylistic choice: datrix_common.migration.schema_snapshot.RdbmsSchemaSnapshot.schema_name is a shared, language-neutral field (the PostgreSQL schema every table and native enum type in this block is placed in) that dotnet's own _fluentmigrator_ops.py imports RdbmsSchemaSnapshot from, yet a grep of that entire file finds zero references to schema_name anywhere -- the field is silently ignored, so a DSL author who declares a non-default Postgres schema on an rdbms block gets their enum types created in the wrong (default) schema for the dotnet target while python honors the declaration correctly.

collapsibility.reason: dotnet's FluentMigrator adapter never reads RdbmsSchemaSnapshot.schema_name for CREATE TYPE emission even though the field is already threaded into that file for table DDL -- a real emission gap fixable by wiring the same schema_name value into _create_enum_type_sql's identifier construction, not a design difference to preserve.

_endpoint_label.reason: dotnet returns the bare endpoint.name when one is declared, falling back to f"{endpoint.method} {endpoint.path}" only when no name exists; python always prefixes the uppercased HTTP method (endpoint.method.upper()) ahead of the identity, and its identity itself falls back through three levels (name, then endpoint.path, then a literal '<unnamed>' sentinel) rather than dotnet's two. Both are purely diagnostic identity strings feeding each package's own build_callable_doc/error-message call sites, not values that reach generated output, so each author chose their own human-readable error-message shape independently.

collapsibility.reason: the divergence is in the diagnostic STRING FORMAT itself (whether the method is always prefixed, whether it's uppercased, and how many fallback levels exist before an unnamed sentinel), not a casing convention, a shared table, or a signature-shape difference -- there is no shared vocabulary or predicate underneath two genuinely different human-readable formats.

_enum_member_default_sql.reason: This is the same enum/kind dispatch-order split already seen in _column_default_sql, propagated one level down: dotnet's outer _column_default_sql resolves default.kind (server_function/generated) BEFORE checking col.type.kind == 'enum', so by the time _enum_member_default_sql runs, dotnet guarantees the default is already a literal (its docstring states this directly) and the function has no server-evaluated branch. typescript's outer _column_default_sql checks the enum type FIRST, before looking at default.kind at all, so its _enum_member_default_sql must itself handle default.kind in _SERVER_EVALUATED_DEFAULT_KINDS internally (routing through call_source_default_to_sql) -- a branch dotnet's sibling function doesn't need. Signatures also diverge for the same reason as _column_default_sql: typescript carries an extra snapshot parameter (used by _snapshot_enum_for_column to look up the enum's declared members from a snapshot-wide registry) and a second sql_dialect string parameter, where dotnet reads the enum's members directly off col.type.values with a single string dialect.

collapsibility.reason: the two functions don't just differ in signature shape -- they differ in which CASES each one is responsible for handling at all (dotnet's is literal-only by construction of its caller's dispatch order; typescript's must also cover server-evaluated defaults), so no shared predicate or signature-alignment fix closes the gap without first unifying the outer dispatch order these two functions are downstream of.

_extract_max_length.reason: All three wrap the same shared `datrix_codegen_common.algorithms.scalar_defaults.extract_max_length`, which takes two optional resolver callables. Dotnet's `test_factory_generator.py` instance method supplies both -- `self._scalar_declaration_for_field` for CustomScalarType lookups and `max_length_from_efcore_column_type` against `self._dotnet_type_map()` for EF Core column-type-derived length -- because it runs inside a generator instance with those resolvers bound. Dotnet's second declaration in `_spec_hook_placeholders.py` is a free function (no generator instance at that call site) that supplies the identical EF-Core resolver but against the module-level `DOTNET_TYPE_MAP` constant and an explicit `scalar_index: Mapping[str, ScalarDeclaration]` parameter instead of `self`. Python passes `scalar_declaration_for=None, max_length_for_scalar_type=None` because python has neither a custom-scalar-index concept nor an EF-Core-style column-type-to-length derivation -- the shared function's own docstring documents this exact `None` case as matching python's pre-hoist behaviour exactly.

_migration_target_name.reason: Byte-identical logic across all three -- `return f"{_MIGRATION_TARGET_NAME} on {dialect}"` (python uses `"%s on %s" % (...)` instead of an f-string, same result) -- differing only in the per-language `_MIGRATION_TARGET_NAME` constant value: `dotnet/FluentMigrator`, `Java/Liquibase`, `Python/Alembic`, each naming that language's actual migration framework so an unrealized-index-kind error tells the author which tool and dialect to fix.

_raise_if_malformed_interpolation_marker.reason: Identical guard condition (`if "#{" in span`) and identical exception type (`TranspilationError`) in both dotnet and python; python's docstring explicitly states it mirrors dotnet's `_raise_if_malformed_interpolation_marker` by file:line reference. The only difference is cosmetic message wording -- dotnet's message is prefixed with `visit_literal: ` for caller context, python's is not -- with both raising the same "found '#{' with no matching '}'" text otherwise.

_realized_index_kinds.reason: Byte-identical bodies and byte-identical docstrings (Args/Returns text matches word-for-word) across dotnet, java, and python: build an empty set, add `INDEX_KIND_SPATIAL` if `dialect` is in the spatial-dialects constant, add `INDEX_KIND_FULLTEXT` if in the fulltext-dialects constant, return a frozenset. The only difference is each file references its own identically-named-in-purpose but differently-named constant (`_SPATIAL_INDEX_DIALECTS`/`_FULLTEXT_INDEX_DIALECTS` in dotnet/java vs `_SPATIAL_MIGRATION_DIALECTS`/`_FULLTEXT_MIGRATION_DIALECTS` in python), all three currently valued `frozenset({"postgresql"})`.

_snapshot_column_for.reason: Near-identical logic (look up `field_name` in `table.fields`, raise `GenerationError` with an 'Available: {sorted list}' hint if missing) in both java and python. The structural difference is the last parameter's type: java threads the shared `ChangeKind` enum itself (`kind: ChangeKind`, read via `kind.value` in the message) since java's call sites still hold the enum; python's call sites pre-resolve it and pass a bare `operation: str` (`change.kind.value` at the call site) instead. Both import the same `datrix_common.migration.differ.ChangeKind` -- this is a parameter-shape choice, not a missing capability.

_snapshot_table_for.reason: Same story as its sibling `_snapshot_column_for`: both look up `entity_name` in `snapshot.migration_tables()` (which already includes CQRS read-model backing tables in both languages) and raise `GenerationError` with a sorted 'Available' list if absent. Java's signature takes the shared `ChangeKind` enum (`kind: ChangeKind`, via `kind.value`); python's takes a pre-resolved `operation: str`. Python's docstring additionally spells out the read-model-table rationale in an Args/Returns/Raises block where java's stays a one-line docstring -- a documentation-verbosity difference, not a logic difference.

emit_doc_block.reason: Python renders a docstring as one delimited literal -- `f"{indent}{_DOCSTRING_DELIMITER}{text}{_DOCSTRING_DELIMITER}"`, a single triple-quote-wrapped string with no per-line marker, because a Python docstring needs none. TypeScript instead builds a multi-line JSDoc block: splits `text` on `\n`, prefixes every non-empty line with `{indent} * ` and every empty line with `{indent} *` (no trailing space), and wraps the whole thing between `{indent}/**` and `{indent} */` -- the C-style block-comment convention JSDoc tooling expects. These are two structurally incompatible comment-block shapes (one string-literal wrap, one line-by-line asterisk-prefixed block), not a formatting variant of the same operation.

collapsibility.reason: a shared renderer would have to know whether to emit a single wrapped literal or a per-line-prefixed block and what that prefix/terminator is -- reconstructing each language's own comment syntax through a parameter, which is the same forbidden per-target branch this hoist chain rejects elsewhere; there is no common line-oriented structure to factor out since python's docstring form has no per-line marker to share with TypeScript's asterisk gutter.

emit_note_block.reason: python's `emit_note_block` reimplements the `#`-prefixed line-splitting inline (`text.split("\n")` + `f"{indent}# {line}"`) rather than calling `PythonSyntaxEmitters.emit_comment`, even though that method exists and delegates to the same shared `_comment_physical_lines`/`_prefix_comment_line` helpers that back `IndentBlockSyntaxEmitters.emit_comment`; typescript's `emit_note_block` instead delegates to `TypeScriptSyntaxEmitters.emit_comment` (inherited from `CBraceSyntaxEmitters`, same shared helpers), explicitly to reuse the same statement-level channel emitter every other statement-level source comment in that package already goes through.

collapsibility.reason: both languages already have access to the identical shared comment-emitting helpers via their own SyntaxEmitters.emit_comment method (confirmed non-defective by datrix-codegen-common's own doc-profile-sanitizer test, whose reference fixture deliberately mirrors python's manual, non-delegating approach and still passes); the divergence is purely which of two already-correct call sites each language's emit_note_block happens to invoke, not a structural gap any listed mechanism collapses.

nested_handler_name.reason: `NestedCollectionRoute` deliberately carries three separate precomputed name fields for exactly this purpose (its own docstring: language generators keep owning how those names become source text) -- dotnet's handler name uses `route.child_plural` (matching ASP.NET Core's REST-collection-plural controller-action convention), java uses `route.child_snake` (singular child-entity form), and typescript uses `route.relationship_alias` (the snake_cased DSL-declared relationship name/alias, which can diverge from the child entity name entirely when a `hasMany` relationship declares an alias).

collapsibility.reason: this isn't a casing split a naming-profile-caser could close -- each language selects a different underlying semantic field (plural child name vs singular child name vs relationship alias) before any casing is applied, and the shared dataclass already precomputes all three specifically so each generator can make that selection independently; there is nothing left to hoist without re-introducing a per-language field-choice parameter into the name-selection logic itself.

nested_handler_names_for_rest_api.reason: Once `nested_handler_name` is called, the surrounding collision-detection body is byte-for-byte identical across all three languages: same `reserved: dict[str, str] = {}` accumulator, same `for route in derived_nested_collection_routes(service): if route.rest_api_name != str(rest_api.name): continue`, same duplicate-name `GenerationError` (with the identical message text). The only other difference is that dotnet local-imports `derived_nested_collection_routes` inside the function body while java/typescript import it at module top -- a dotnet-specific import-ordering artifact, not a behavioral difference.

collapsibility.reason: with the per-language nested_handler_name selection already isolated to its own classified entry, the surrounding collision-detection loop is already byte-identical across all three targets, parameterized only by the rest_api and the name-selector function -- nothing structurally blocks hoisting it into datrix_codegen_common today; the hoist itself is not yet landed.

persisted_enum_member_literal.reason: python's SQLAlchemy `Enum(PyEnumClass)` mapping persists the enum's MEMBER NAME (no `values_callable` emitted), so `persisted_enum_member_literal` always returns `to_snake_case(value.name)` and never reads any declared `value(...)` at all; typescript's MikroORM `@Enum({items})` binds the enum's VALUES, so its version (via the shared `_persisted_literal` helper) reads `value.explicit_value` first and only falls back to `to_snake_case(member_name)` when no DSL `value(...)` was declared -- e.g. `Standard : value(1)` persists as `1` in typescript but as `standard` in python. Two ORMs bind a different half of the same member/value pair.

collapsibility.reason: there is no shared per-language map or casing swap that reconciles this -- python's function structurally never consults a declared value at all (a fixed one-input rule dictated by SQLAlchemy's own persistence model), while typescript's is a two-input value-with-fallback rule; collapsing them would mean growing python a dead branch it can never exercise, which is importing one ORM's persistence semantics into the other's generator, not a hoist.

sanitize_doc_text.reason: python's version splits BOTH triple-quote delimiter flavors (`"""` and `'''`, since a Python docstring rendered with one could be broken by a body containing the other) and additionally neutralizes a trailing odd run of backslashes -- a real Python-specific hazard, since a non-raw string literal's trailing `\` would escape the first quote character of the closing `"""` delimiter `emit_doc_block` appends; typescript's version only splits the single `*/` block-comment terminator and has no backslash-run handling at all, because a `/** ... */` JSDoc comment has no string-literal escape mechanism for a trailing backslash to exploit.

collapsibility.reason: the hazard sets are structurally different in kind, not just count -- python's docstring is a string-literal construct with an escape-character grammar (hence the trailing-backslash rule and two delimiter flavors), while typescript's block comment has no escape grammar at all (hence neither concern exists there); no shared vocabulary/casing/table mechanism collapses 'has an escape grammar' vs 'has none'.

service_declares_keyword_bearing_enum.reason: Both bodies are functionally identical AST-closure walks with zero language-specific logic: dotnet factors the per-enum check into a private `_enum_declares_keyword` helper (reused a third time by `_first_keyword_bearing_enum_name`'s error-message lookup), while java inlines the identical `any(ev.keywords for ev in enum.values)` expression twice directly in the loop instead of factoring it out. Both walk the SAME shared `collect_enums_for_service`/`collect_block_enums_for_service` closure imported from `datrix_codegen_common.algorithms.enum_collection` and read the same language-agnostic AST attribute (`EnumValue.keywords`) -- no C#/Java-specific fact appears anywhere in either function body.

collapsibility.reason: both bodies already walk the identical shared enum-collection closure and test the identical language-agnostic AST attribute with zero remaining per-language fact -- java's only divergence from dotnet is an un-factored inline expression rather than a private helper, so nothing structurally blocks folding both into one shared predicate; the hoist itself is not yet landed.

service_needs_domain_exceptions.reason: Three declarations, not a real 3-way disagreement. dotnet's `gendsl/file_builders.py` declaration is a thin scope-rebinding wrapper: genDSL's executor binds `when call` targets by matching the callee's own parameter names against its scope, and genDSL's domain-scope key for the Application AST node is `application`, not `app`, so the wrapper exists purely to rename that one parameter before delegating unchanged to dotnet's real logic in `error_response_generator.service_needs_domain_exceptions`, which is a FOUR-way disjunction including `service_references_builtin_exception` -- a DSL-body walk for a bare `ValidationError(...)`/`AuthorizationError(...)`/`AuthenticationError(...)` raise, needed because dotnet's `throw ValidationError(...)` lowers to a named, DSL-referenceable exception class. Java's version is a THREE-way disjunction with no such walk, because java's `throw ValidationError(...)` never lowers to `ServiceValidationError` at all; it lowers to `ResponseStatusException` (handler scope) or `IllegalStateException` (job scope) instead, so java has no DSL-body raise site for `ServiceValidationError` to account for.

collapsibility.reason: the dotnet-internal split is a pure parameter-name rebinding for genDSL's scope-matching convention with zero behavioral difference (exactly what signature-alignment would collapse in isolation), but that mechanism can't also absorb the dotnet-vs-java gap, which is a genuine difference in disjunct count driven by where each language's own transpiler routes a bare domain-exception raise; a shared predicate would need a per-language extra-disjunct flag reconstructing a fact each language's own lowering pipeline already encodes, so no single listed mechanism covers both gaps and 'none' is the honest fit.

_active_templates.reason: dotnet defers crypto-sign template resolution behind a _CRYPTO_SIGN_PENDING sentinel so a deployment-free DotnetHelperGenerator (e.g. GEO-family builders) never needs a resolved deployment just to list active templates; python resolves the crypto-sign template eagerly via _crypto_sign_template_for_platform(); java's feature table has no crypto-sign branch in this method at all.

collapsibility.reason: resolution TIMING (lazy sentinel-deferred vs eager vs branch entirely absent) is driven by each generator's own instantiation lifecycle (deployment-scoped vs deployment-free vs provider-identity plugin chain), not a template shape, casing, or type-map difference any listed mechanism collapses.

_aggregate_comparison_violation.reason: each converts the DSL parameter name through its own identifier-casing key function (dotnet keeps the raw DSL name, java maps through _param_java_key, python maps through _param_python_key) before indexing its own {csharp,java,python}_types map and raising a language-named 'No X type for contract parameter' error.

collapsibility.reason: same finding as the numeric-family violation cluster this belongs to: each language derives its literal/args shape from its OWN AST/type-name vocabulary, with no shared classification key underneath the worked example's assumed wrapper.

_apply_nosql_chain_step.reason: Each target builds its where-filter through its own NoSQL filter-syntax constant (DOTNET_NOSQL_FILTER_SYNTAX/JAVA_NOSQL_FILTER_SYNTAX/PY_NOSQL_FILTER_SYNTAX) and raises that language's own exception type (TranspilationError in dotnet/python, GenerationError in java) -- each renders a different MongoDB driver's query-builder call shape (C# Mongo driver filter builder vs Java Mongo driver vs Motor). The where-branch additionally unwraps its own empty-object sentinel differently (python slices [1:-1] off a brace literal, java slices past 'Map.of(' and drops an empty remainder, dotnet appends the expression whole), the sort accumulator differs in TYPE (a pre-rendered string in python/java, a list of parts in dotnet), java alone interpolates the entity name into every diagnostic, and dotnet's signature takes no entity_name at all.

collapsibility.reason: the dispatch skeleton is genuinely the same, but every branch body differs in sentinel unwrapping, accumulator type, exception class and message text at once; a shared version would need a parameter per branch plus a message-format parameter, which is the forbidden per-target conditional wearing a keyword-argument costume.
